reframing_when: The question seeks confirmation of an existing belief without defining what evidence would disprove it — the question is designed to succeed rather than to learn.
The question asks 'is X true?' without asking 'what would prove X false?' — the falsification frame is missing.
The question's implicit assumptions have not been spelled out concretely enough to be tested — the 'what would you have to believe?' analysis has not been done.

The question assumes a plan or strategy will work without identifying the specific conditions under which it would fail — the sensitivity analysis question ('by how much would assumptions need to change for this to be wrong?') is absent.
reframing_move: Invert the question toward disproof: instead of 'will X work?', ask 'what specific condition would prove X wrong, and can we test for that condition now?' — the hypothesis pyramid reframe makes assumptions concrete enough to break.
curation_note: Falsifiability is a reframing tool because it converts questions designed to confirm into questions designed to learn. The source is explicit: the Feynman standard ('lean over backwards to figure out where you could be wrong'), the hypothesis pyramid (sub-hypotheses specific enough to be disproven), and the WTWHTB test all operate on question structure. Distinct from inversion — falsifiability specifically targets the epistemic quality of the question, not just its direction.

reframing_when.note: All four activations grounded: confirmation-seeking (Feynman standard), missing falsification frame (core principle), unspelled assumptions (WTWHTB test), and absent sensitivity analysis (assumption change threshold question).

frame_patterns_challenged.note: Borrowed premise: inherited assumptions made testable by spelling them out. Counterfactual suppression: the disconfirmation question surfaces the paths the question's frame suppresses.
